list.listitem: Look for tick-borne disease in patients with a flu-like illness "out of season". C
An erythema migrans rash in a patient from a Lyme disease endemic region is sufficient reason to begin empiric antibiotic treatment for Lyme disease. C

When the clinical setting is not in an endemic area or the diagnosis is unclear for another reason, move forward with a two-tiered approach beginning with antibody testing with enzyme immunoassay or immunofluorescence assay, followed by confirmatory enzyme immunoassay if positive or equivocal.C

Prevention of Lyme disease and other vector-borne diseases is best accomplished by a combination of avoidance of contact with vectors, use of repellants, appropriate clothing, at least daily whole-body inspections while in risk areas and removal of attached ticks as soon as possible. C
Prophylaxis for asymptomatic patients with tick bite only recommended if specific criteria are met. B
Preferred oral antibiotics for symptomatic patients are doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime axetil ( and ). B

background.definition: Lyme disease is a multiphase, multi-system, tick-borne zoonosis caused by Borrelia species, which is transmitted by the bite of the tick of Ixodes scapularis, I. pacificus, I. persulcatus or I. ricinus .

list.listitem: Incidence ranges from less than 1/100,000 in low incidence areas (such as Colorado) to over 68/100,000 in high incidence areas.
Highest incidence is in Northeast, mid-Atlantic, and northern midwest of United States. Cases have risen dramatically since 2021.
Global seroprevelance of Borrelia burgdorferi is 14.5%.
Disease occurs in distinct and geographically limited foci ().
In setting of climate change, incidence and geographic distribution of cases of Lyme disease has increased over time.
Cases peak in first week of July.
Lyme disease is the most frequently reported vector-borne disease in the US.
Lyme disease accounts for 82% of vector-borne diseases but other tickborne illnesses such as anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, Rickettsioses, and babesiosis are increasing in number each year.

Lyme disease is caused by spirochete infection with one of the five species of the Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato species complex. Two of these species, Borrelia burgdorferi and Borrelia mayoii, are endemic to the United States.
A Lyme disease-like illness with atypical rash and different clinical features may represent infection by a different species within the species complex.
Recurrence of Lyme disease represents infection by a different strain rather than reinfection.
Borrelia burgdorferi are transmitted to the skin of the host by the bite of an infected tick, Ixodes scapularis or I. pacificus in the U.S and I. persulcatus or I. ricinus in Europe.

The bacteria disseminate preferentially to certain target organs (skin, heart, synovium, nervous system) where they can evoke an immunologically mediated inflammatory response resulting in tissue injury.
Screening for Lyme disease is not recommended. C

Prevention includes avoiding tick-infested areas, wearing light-colored, long-sleeve shirt, long pants, pants tucked into socks, and washing clothing in hot water after use. Use DEET repellant for skin and permethrin for clothing, and perform a "tick check" at least once daily and remove any attached ticks. C
For patients with a tick bite meeting all high risk criteria, single dose doxycycline can prevent Lyme disease (NNT = 50). B
Routine use of antimicrobial prophylaxis or serologic testing after recognized tick bite is not recommended. C
Screening for Lyme disease is not recommended.
Testing of ticks for infectious agents is not recommended.
Avoid exposure to vector ticks (outdoor sites in endemic areas, especially with undisturbed vegetation).
Wear protective clothing (long sleeves and long pants, light in color with pants tucked into socks) and use tick repellants or wear permethrin coated clothing.
Approved repellents include DEET (diethylmetatoluamide), picardin, oil of lemon eucalyptus, 2-undecanone, IR3535 and para-menthane-diol (PMD).
Removal of ticks before 24 hours of attachment greatly reduces risk of disease transmission.
Bathing less than two hours after outdoor activity reduces risk of infection in endemic areas.
Permethrin treatment of clothing is recommended for prolonged or frequent exposure to high risk environments.
Check entire body for ticks daily ("tick checks") and promptly remove any attached ticks.
Topical azithromycin was not shown to be more effective than placebo in preventing asymptomatic seroconversion within 72 hours of a confirmed tick bite.
A vaccine against Lyme borreliosis is in early clinical trials.
Assess the pretest probability of a patient with suspected Lyme disease on the basis of clinical signs and symptoms and likelihood of exposure. C
Lyme disease may be diagnosed without serologic testing in a patient from a highly endemic area with erythema migrans. C

When the clinical setting is not an endemic area or the diagnosis is unclear for another reason, move forward with a two tiered approach beginning with antibody testing with enzyme immunoassay or immunofluorescence assay, followed by confirmatory enzyme immunoassay if initial test positive or equivocal.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Erythema at the site of tick attachment which develops and fades rapidly (36-48 hrs)
Cellulitis is usually tender, erythema migrans is minimally or non-tender, lacks central clearing
Mucosal lesions do not occur with Lyme and palms and soles are generally spared
EM-like lesion in patient from an area not endemic for Lyme, milder illness, fewer lesions
Rarely bilateral except in Lyme disease
Brief, recurrent attacks more common with Lyme, initial presentation must r/o bacterial cause
Thin, raised borders with scale, spread over weeks/months, +KOH
Raised lesions, prominent pruritus, sudden appearance and evanescence

Differential.Differential_Name: Reaction to insect or spider bite
Differential.Differential_Features: Bite often recalled, reaction develops quickly, usually on exposed areas of body
Rapid onset of rash within 6-12 h of exposure, severe pruritus, vesicles
Papules or nodules in a circular distribution up to several centimeters in diameter, no prodrome
Circular papular lesions from 2-10 cm in diameter with pruritus and scaling

list.listitem: For surveillance purposes only, a reportable case of Lyme disease is defined as: (1) clinician-diagnosed erythema migrans equal to or greater than 5cm OR (2) at least one objective late manifestation (that is, musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, or neurological) with laboratory evidence of infection.

7 to 10 days after tick bite (range 3-30 days), approximately three-quarters of infected patients develop the early, localized form of the disease; characterized by erythema migrans with or without an influenza-like syndrome.
Clinical diagnosis by erythema migrans may not be reliable in children.
Influenza "out of season" may be a tick-borne disease, West Nile virus infection or Avian influenza (if the patient has travelled to an Avian influenza endemic region and handled sick or dead birds).

Early disseminated disease occurs weeks to months (average 21 days) after initial illness and is characterized by secondary annular lesions, continued influenza-like symptoms and one or several target organ system symptoms/signs (brief recurrent oligo- or monoarticular large joint arthritis, Bell's palsy, meningitis, AV block).
In Europe, untreated chronic Lyme caused by B. afzelli can cause chronic skin changes, called acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans.

Co-infection occurs in up to 10% of patients. Human granulocytic anaplasmosis and/or babesiosis present with prolonged influenza-like illness that fails to respond to anti-Borrelial therapy. The EM rash may resolve, but fevers may persist beyond 24 to 48 hours of antibiotic therapy.
In children, the Rule of 7's (absence of each of the following: ≥7 days of headache, any cranial neuritis or ≥70% cerebrospinal fluid mononuclear cell) can accurately rule out Lyme meningitis.

Patients with EM rash in an area of high incidence should be treated empirically without laboratory testing, as the risk of a false negative enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) is high, especially early in the disease.

For any situation other than that mentioned above, follow the CDC recommended two tier approach beginning with an enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or immunofluorescence assay (IFA). If positive or equivocal, this should be followed by EIA .
If available, the second-tier EIA may be more specific than Western blot and EIA is the preferred second-tier test.
The erythema migrans rash can be biopsied and evaluated by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for B. burgdorferi.

When there is concern for neuroborreliosis, serum antibody testing is preferred over PCR or culture of CSF. If CSF is sampled, simultaneous serum and CSF antibody measurement is recommended in order to obtain a CSF: serum antibody index.
When there is concern for Lyme arthritis, serum antibody testing is preferred over PCR or culture of the blood or synovial fluid.
If synovial fluid is sampled for confirmation, consider PCR testing, rather than culture, of synovial fluid in addition to serum testing.

In a small cohort study, a commercially available, rapid serum immunoassay (C6 enzyme immunoassay) was found to be sensitive and specific for diagnosis of Lyme arthritis. This appears to help distinguish between Lyme arthritis and septic arthritis in children presenting to the ED in Lyme endemic areas.

In a cohort of 735 children with monoarthritis, none of the 450 children with procalcitonin < 0.5, CRP < 0.6 mg/dl, and positive Lyme C6 EIA had a non-Lyme bacterial musculoskeletal infection (septic arthritis, pyomyositis, or osteomyelitis).
History of significant exposure in a Lyme disease endemic area is key (). See .

If the patient is asymptomatic, do not treat. Provide prophylaxis if three criteria are met: 1) the tick is identified as Ixodes species; 2) the exposure took place in an area with endemic Lyme (image 1); 3) the tick was attached for at least 36 hours. Prophylaxis must be initiated within 72 hours of tick removal.
If EM is present and the exposure took place in a Lyme endemic setting (>20% ticks infected), then treat according the the guidelines described in the Drug Therapy section and in .

For any situation other than that mentioned above, follow the CDC recommended two tier approach beginning with an enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or immunofluorescence assay (IFA). If the EIA or IFA is positive or equivocal and the patient has been symptomatic for one month or less, order a follow up confirmatory test (EIA preferred). If the initial sample is negative, then follow up with a convalescent phase serum sample at 2-3 week after initial collection.
Consider antibiotic administration while awaiting test results depending on clinical picture.
Preferred oral antibiotics are doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime axetil (). B
Alternative oral antibiotics include macrolides like azithromycin. B

Because of the potential severity of other tick-borne diseases with similar early presentations, empiric therapy with doxycycline or other first-line antibiotic may be indicated while diagnostic testing is obtained. C
shows the available drug regimens for patients in whom treatment is indicated, with the duration of therapy shown in .
Children can be treated with doxycycline, without regard to age, if duration of treatment is <21 days.
A small randomized trial found doxycycline, amoxicillin, and penicillin had similar efficacy for treatment of erythema migrans.
An open label trial randomized 300 adults with erythema migrans to 7 or 14 days of oral doxycycline. They found no difference in outcomes between the groups (3% vs 2% with persistent rash).

A network meta-analysis concluded that for patients with early cutaneous Lyme borreliosis (LB), a short course of doxycycline (10-14 days) is as effective as alternative drugs or longer courses. Amoxicillin 500 mg 3 times daily or cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily for 14 days are both reasonable alternatives according to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and this analysis. The preferred oral drug is doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily in non-pregnant patients.
If intolerant of above antibiotics, azithromycin for 7 days is alternative.
Doxycycline for a duration of 2 weeks has similar efficacy as compared to ceftriaxone IV daily 14 days for treatment of Lyme neuroborreliosis.
The preferred parenteral antibiotic is ceftriaxone 2 grams daily.
After recognized tick bite, routine use of antibiotic prophylaxis or serologic testing is not recommended.

Prophylaxis for patients with an asymptomatic tick bite with single dose doxycycline (200 mg for adults and 4 mg/kg for children) should be given only when all of the following circumstances exist: tick from Ixodes species has been attached for at least 36 hours, prophylaxis can be started within 72 hours of tick removal, and the local rate of tick infection with B. burgdorferi is greater than 20%.

Prophylaxis with single dose of doxycycline (200 mg once or 4 mg/kg) administered within 72 hours of tick removal may reduce the risk of Lyme borreliosis (NNT=51) in Europe where other Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lata genospecies are endemic. Routine prophylaxis in the United States is not recommended unless meeting previously listed criteria.
Prolonged Lyme disease antibiotic treatment for persistent symptoms has not been found to be effective in multiple randomized trials.

A meta-analysis found no difference between beta-lactams and doxycycline at 12 months for patients with residual neurological symptoms. There was also no benefit to extended antibiotic treatment of neurologic symptoms. Finally, addition of steroids was not effective for patients with facial palsy.

An RCT of 239 patients with persistent Lyme associated symptoms compared 2 weeks of ceftriaxone versus 2 weeks of ceftriaxone followed by either 12 weeks of doxycycline or clarithromycin/hydroxychloroquine. There was no difference in any neurocognitive outcomes between groups, with all patients improving similarly.
Arthroscopic synovectomy for persistent synovitis.
For Lyme carditis, temporary pacemaker insertion is recommended over permanent pacemaker for high degree atrioventricular or complete heart block.
Persons with symptoms searching for a disease may be drawn to "chronic Lyme disease" as a diagnosis.
No data support Borrelia as a cause of chronic symptomatology.

Many proprietary laboratories offer Lyme disease testing beyond the CDC-recommended two-step protocol. No well-controlled studies support the use of these alternative testing protocols for diagnosis or to direct therapy.
Lyme arthritis may require PT/OT intervention, but radiographic erosions of cartilage or bone are rare.
See for recommendations regarding duration of therapy.
Hospitalize in cases of high grade heart block (PR interval >300), symptoms of myocarditis, arrhythmia, or meningitis.
Approximately 20% of Lyme disease episodes resolve spontaneously. B
More than 90% of treated Lyme disease episodes completely resolve with standard antibiotic therapy. Symptom resolution with macrolide therapy is 80%.B
Previous reports found 20% of untreated patients experience complications, most commonly arthritis. Due to early recognition, this percentage has likely declined in recent years.
Between 4-10% of untreated Lyme disease patients develop carditis.
Approximately 15% will develop neurologic abnormalities (primarily Bell's palsy).
More than 90% of treated early Lyme cases resolve without sequelae.
Follow-up serologic testing for cure is not recommended.
The probability of Lyme disease transmission is near zero if attached Ixodes ticks are recognized and removed before 36 hours of attachment.
Ixodes (deer) tick nymphs are very small (sesame seed size or smaller), so must be searched for carefully.
Localized, early disease: amoxicillin 500mg PO q8h or cefuroxime axetil 500 mg PO q12h for 14 days.
Clinicians can also consider doxycycline after careful discussion with patients based upon a systematic review demonstrating no harms.
Other manifestations: penicillin G, 20,000,000 U IV, daily in divided doses for 14 to 28 days or ceftriaxone, 2g daily for 14 to 28 days.

feature.caption: Lyme Disease Diagnostic Strategies.
feature.feature_body:
Clinical Presentation Diagnostic Strategy
Lyme disease endemic region (prevalence of Borrelia burgdorferi infected ticks >20%)
Symptoms/signs suggesting disseminated Lyme disease Treat presumptively and obtain serologic testing
Flu-like illness with erythema migrans rash Diagnose Lyme disease clinically, no laboratory testing necessary
Prolonged constitutional symptoms suggesting Lyme disease Serologic testing (2-step approach)
Positive acute phase immunoassay Diagnose Lyme disease
Negative acute phase immunoassay Not diagnostic, proceed with convalescent serum EIA
Positive convalescent phase immunoassay Diagnose Lyme disease
Negative acute and convalescent phase immunoassay Do not diagnose Lyme disease
Lyme disease nonendemic region
No erythema migrans Do not test for Lyme disease
Erythema migrans Two-step test for Lyme disease
Prolonged, nonspecific, unexplained symptoms (>2 weeks) Consider 2-step test
